title: The dirty truth about office politics (school never taught you this secret to succeed).
summary: Prompted by a mailbag question, Jean and Cherie discuss how to become a top performer in the corporate world: the mindset of persistence and growth, the necessity of allies and a supportive boss, emotional intelligence as the skill that takes you to the executive level, and the unspoken reality of office politics. They share personal stories (financial-aid struggles in college, recession-era Goldman rejections, a toxic seatmate at Goldman, a salary-sharing spreadsheet at LinkedIn) and conclude that top performers unapologetically ask for what they need and advocate for themselves.

ideas.idea: Persistence is a free trait available to anyone: if you don't get an answer, a no-answer is not an answer yet, so keep emailing until you get a response.
ideas.detail: As a Columbia freshman, Cherie emailed Dr. Sia's microfluidics lab three or four times (she remembers six) with no reply until he finally invited her in for an interview; repeated follow-ups demonstrate determination before you've ever had an interaction with someone.

ideas.idea: Traits like determination and a growth mindset cannot be developed by sitting still; they are earned by being rejected repeatedly and getting back up.
ideas.detail: Jean applied for finance internships through the 2007-2010 recession, was rejected by Goldman Sachs multiple times, and still ended up with a Goldman offer out of undergrad; you must believe success can come, or there is no point in trying, and you must not take rejection personally.

ideas.idea: Top performance is not just doing good work; it requires people who will shine a light on you and make sure your work is recognized.
ideas.detail: Cherie cites having male allies in a male-dominated workplace; promotion depends not only on your boss buying in but on everyone on the promotion committee who has power over you, so perception matters.

ideas.idea: People in the workplace are far more self-oriented than a new grad assumes, and some will actively undermine you, so learn this early rather than through a painful lesson.
ideas.detail: Jean says she was naive for years, assuming everyone was working toward the team's stated goal, without considering colleagues' private incentives that run counter to the team's goals or to her success; it is usually not personal, you may just be in their way.

ideas.idea: It is very hard to be a top performer in the corporate world without the support of your boss, so find people who believe in you and never pin your whole self-view on one person.
ideas.detail: Jean had one boss she would 'walk through walls' for and another who undermined her in ways she calls traumatic; when the boss relationship is bad, seek a second, third and fourth opinion from people you respect who can reflect back what you're doing well.

ideas.idea: If you are stuck with a bad boss in a political situation, either learn what you can from it or get out so you have agency to put yourself in a better one.
ideas.detail: The hosts acknowledge much is out of your control and leaving is hard in today's job market, but that is the reality of the options.

ideas.idea: Intelligence gets you into the room, but emotional intelligence is the skill that takes you to the executive or VP level.
ideas.detail: Cherie cites studies naming EQ as the number-one skill for advancement and Travis Bradberry's 'Emotional Intelligence 2.0' as a way to test and grow it; the best performers read the room and understand how others feel.

ideas.idea: Once you lead a team, the majority of your time goes to people problems, which will be either the death of you or the making of you.
ideas.detail: The hosts say team dynamics start to show at about five people and dominate a manager's time at twelve or more.

ideas.idea: Manage teams with a T-shaped philosophy: double down on each person's one or two standout skills and make them the team's tutor for it, rather than forcing everyone to be well-rounded.
ideas.detail: Jean ran her teams this way so everyone was a top performer in a niche; being acknowledged for a strength makes people more receptive to improving weaknesses, seniors learn from juniors, and it creates more surface area than the zero-sum game of everyone chasing well-roundedness, though basic role requirements still must be met.

ideas.idea: At the executive level, influence depends on intuiting the true drivers, motivations and core beliefs behind another executive's behavior and shaping your approach to conversations accordingly.
ideas.detail: Jean says you must deliberately take time to think about what each person actually wants before meetings in order to reach a broader meeting of the minds.

ideas.idea: In political corporate environments, people's stated desires may overlap only about 15 percent with their true desires, so learn to read what is under the surface.
ideas.detail: The hosts say that at startups and small companies everyone is aligned on company success and there is less obfuscation, but past a certain size everything becomes political and most people will work at a big company at some point.

ideas.idea: The meritocracy formula of school (study hard, ace the SATs, get into a good school) does not carry over to the corporate world, which has variables nobody teaches you about.
ideas.detail: Both hosts entered the workforce with 'rose-colored glasses' and were hit hard because their family had no corporate background and no one in college explains how corporations actually function; politics exists even in academia over first-name authorship and grants.

ideas.idea: An immigrant or first-generation upbringing of deferring to adults and authority figures can hinder your career because you don't learn to talk to seniors as equals or question them.
ideas.detail: Jean contrasts herself with white friends who grew up 'shooting the shit' with their parents' friends; Cherie wishes she had questioned teachers more in school instead of absorbing everything unquestioningly.

ideas.idea: Top performers ask for what they need, unapologetically but respectfully, because the worst outcome is a 'no' and the upside is far greater than not asking.
ideas.detail: In her first job at Goldman, Jean agonized for weeks over a colleague who kicked her under the table before finally asking her VP to swap seats; he said yes immediately, she sat next to a normal associate, and her life improved '50X', leaving her wondering why fear and a scarcity mindset kept her from asking sooner.

ideas.idea: Practice asking for things at a micro level so you have the reps in when a high-stakes ask like a salary negotiation comes up.
ideas.detail: Jean once forced herself through a challenge of asking for things, including asking for the whole bag of sample chips at Trader Joe's and getting it; harmless low-stakes asks are a form of rejection exposure therapy.

ideas.idea: No one will care more about your career than you do, so you must advocate for yourself, especially in salary negotiations; a good boss is only a close second.
ideas.detail: Being a top performer also means being compensated commensurately for it.

ideas.idea: Share compensation data with peers at your level so you have data points to strengthen your salary negotiation narrative.
ideas.detail: Cherie's LinkedIn associate product manager cohort, at her friend Logan's suggestion, filled out a Google Sheet with promotions, bonuses and salaries, a private Glassdoor; cite the data without naming individuals, because 'he got paid X so I should' is a bad look and her boss told her so. Jean once discovered a direct report had a higher base salary than she did.

ideas.idea: Financial independence is the antidote to the powerlessness of early hardship, and the drive to be a top performer often comes from never wanting to be in that position again.
ideas.detail: Jean rediscovered sophomore-year emails with her college financial aid office when she thought she'd have to drop out, worked many jobs (tutor, museum security guard, RA, research assistant), and says nothing will ever be as hard as that time of having no control; both sisters are driven so neither they nor their children face that again.

ideas.idea: Most creators fail because they give up; the first 100 episodes of 20VC never broke 1,000 plays and now it gets 1,000 plays in 90 seconds.
ideas.detail: Jean found Harry Stebbings' post a helpful benchmark while bemoaning that their episodes don't break 10K views, and saw it as a meta example of why sharing your vulnerable early struggles helps others keep going.

ideas.idea: Going viral has a toxic side: a near-million-view video eventually reaches misogynistic corners of the internet, and you can logic your way through hate comments without it ceasing to hurt.
ideas.detail: Cherie's dating-response video drew abusive comments; celebrities have teams scrub non-constructive comments and distill the rest like a performance review, and Hasan Minhaj's bit says critics should put their government name and photo to what they say.

ideas.idea: Offline community, such as alumni networks, is a grounding counterweight to life online.
ideas.detail: Cherie served on the executive team of Columbia in Tech in San Francisco and is now organizing Columbia alumni in Los Angeles alongside Stanford alumni events; she enjoys bringing people together and calls it a safe space.
